content: The Sandbox tree, scientifically known as Hura crepitans (synonym: Hura brasiliensis Wild.), is an evergreen tree belonging to the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae). It is native to tropical regions of North and South America, particularly within the Amazon Rainforest. This tree is easily identified by its numerous dark, pointed spines and smooth brown bark. Due to these spines, it has earned the nickname Monkey no-climb. The Sandbox tree can grow up to 100 feet in height, and its large, ovate leaves can reach up to two feet in width. It is a monoecious species, meaning it has both male and female flowers on the same tree. The red flowers lack petals; male flowers grow on elongated spikes, while female flowers are solitary and located in the axils of the leaves. The fruit of the Sandbox tree is a large capsule that undergoes explosive dehiscence. When the fruit ripens, it forcefully ejects seeds, which can be propelled as far as 100 meters (328 feet). This explosive dispersal mechanism has led to the tree being colloquially referred to as the Dynamite tree, named for the loud sound produced when the fruit splits into segments. The tree thrives in wet soil and prefers partial shade, partial sun, or full sun. It is often cultivated for its shade-providing properties. The milky, caustic sap of the tree has been reportedly used by fishermen to poison fish. Additionally, the wood of the tree, marketed under the name hura, is utilized in furniture production. Furthermore, Hura crepitans is sometimes used as an additive in certain preparations of the hallucinogenic drink Ayahuasca.
